title: M365 BEC: malicious inbox rule hiding financial correspondence

source.telemetry: Microsoft 365 Unified Audit Log (Exchange Online mailbox audit)
source.detection: Correlation: anomalous sign-in followed by New-InboxRule within the same session
source.provenance_note: This scenario is NOT from Wazuh or Sysmon. Inbox-rule abuse is only visible in the M365 Unified Audit Log, so the fields below mirror an Exchange Online audit record rather than endpoint telemetry. Representing it as a Wazuh alert would misrepresent where this detection actually comes from.

intel.summary: Attackers do not exploit their way into M365, they sign in with a valid session obtained through AiTM phishing or credential theft. The single most common persistence step that follows is a server-side inbox rule that auto-files or forwards anything matching financial keywords, so the legitimate user never sees the fraudulent thread.
intel.why_this_matters: A password reset alone does not remove an inbox rule. If the rule is missed, the attacker keeps visibility into invoice and wire traffic after the account is supposedly recovered.
observed_kill_chain: AiTM phishing page proxies the real M365 login and captures the session token
Attacker replays the session, bypassing MFA entirely
New-InboxRule created to move financial keywords to a rarely-checked folder
Fraudulent wire-transfer thread proceeds invisibly to the real mailbox owner

alert.description: M365 BEC: inbox rule created to hide financial keywords immediately after anomalous sign-in

fields.SubjectOrBodyContainsWords: invoice; wire; payment; ACH; remittance; bank detail
fields.PrecedingSignIn: SessionId 8f2c4a19 -- token replay, MFA claim present but not freshly satisfied

analyst_note: Rule name is a single character or blank in most real BEC cases -- it renders as near-invisible in the Outlook rules UI. MarkAsRead plus StopProcessingRules together are the strongest single indicator that this rule exists to hide mail rather than organise it.
